chapters.summary: Chair De La Rosa frames the hearing around the FDNY EMS Local 2507 reminder that clinical death begins after four minutes. She describes the August 18 outage where Bronx PSAC 2 call takers could not hear callers for approximately seven hours, affecting about 1,700 calls, with as many as 400 callers never connected. She attributes the cause to a Motorola Solutions software update.
chapters.title: Chair De La Rosa opens with urgency of 911 and the August 18 outage

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to our hearing.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Carmen De La Rosa and I am the Chair of the Committee on Technology.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I'm happy to be joined by my colleagues, Chair Areola, Chair Feliz, and Chair Brewer, in holding this joint hearing on examining New York City's 911 emergency system outage.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I want to begin with the words of FDNY EMS Local 2507, delivered before this Council at a similar hearing.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Clinical death begins after four minutes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Biological death begins after six minutes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And as Local 2507 reminds us, in this modern era, emergency systems are designed to work diligently in seconds because when a life is on the line, there is no time to waste, and every minute counts.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: However, in the early mornings of August 18th, for approximately seven hours, a part of New York City's 911 system failed as call takers at the Bronx Public Safety Answering Center 2 could not hear callers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: According to the New York Times, approximately 1,700 calls were affected and as many as 400 callers had not been connected with a 911 at all.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: New Yorkers were neither informed about the outage nor instructed to text 911 or call back while it was happening.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Mayor Mamdani has since stated that the cost was a software

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: update by OTI's vendor, Motorola Solutions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Ironically, Motorola tells its public safety customers on its website, when someone calls 911, every second counts.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And if something is broken, we need to fix it and not tomorrow.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa notes this was not an isolated incident, citing three Fire CAD outages and three EMS CAD outages in 2022, a human error disruption that October, and 2025 staffing shortages causing 911 callers to hear recorded hold messages. She emphasizes 911 is not an ordinary computer system.
chapters.title: Chair De La Rosa recounts history of 911 system outages

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We need to fix it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: On August 18, New Yorkers lost not seconds, but hours.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The system was fixed seven hours later.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Sadly, this was not an isolated warning.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In 2022, the council heard that fire CAD experienced three unexpected outages, while EMS CAD experienced three outages.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: That October, human error caused another major disruption to FDNY's emergency dispatch system.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And more recently, in 2025, staffing shortages have caused some 911 callers to hear a recorded message telling them to hold because every operator is busy.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa states the hearing aims to learn what happened, why the public was not informed, what safeguards existed and failed, and what redundancy, testing, staffing, and accountability are needed. She welcomes testimony from FDNY, NYPD, OTI, advocates, and experts.
chapters.title: Chair De La Rosa outlines hearing goals and questions for agencies

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: No complex system will ever be perfect.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Software can fail.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: People can make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Networks can be overwhelmed by volume of calls.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But 911 is not an ordinary computer system.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It is the number New Yorkers call on the worst day of their lives.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And we need to treat it with all of that seriousness.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Today, we want to learn what happened, why the public was not immediately informed, what safeguards exist and fail.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: and what redundancy testing, staffing, and accountability are necessary to make sure that the next technological failure does not become a tragedy.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing testimony from the FDNY, NYPD, and the Office of Technology and Innovation, advocates and experts.

chapters.summary: Chair Ariola of the Fire and Emergency Management Committee thanks co-chairs and describes the August outage as highly alarming. She outlines the hearing's focus on how FDNY and EMS dispatch systems were impacted, total number of affected emergencies, and training for personnel to handle disruptions.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola opens on impact of 911 outage on emergency response

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Joann-Ariola, and I am the Chair to the Committee on Fire and Emergency Management.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I want to thank my fellow colleagues, Chairs Brewer, Felice, and De La Rosa, for co-chairing this hearing today on the city's 911 outage that occurred last month.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I also want to thank representatives of the administration and the public for attending today's hearing, as well as

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: my fellow colleagues who are here today.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: As New Yorkers, we know the operation of emergency response services within a densely populated urban area is extremely challenging, and that it is when all aspects of our 911 system are functional.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: As was stated earlier, the August outage of our city's 911 system is highly alarming.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: This disruption impacted the safety of New Yorkers not only by limiting the ability to receive emergency calls, but also to respond to these calls.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It is paramount that we, as a city, provide life-saving responses to fire and medical emergencies and ensure life-saving services are promptly delivered as needed.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: During today's hearing, we want to learn about how both FDNY and EMS dispatch systems were impacted during the outage.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: What were the total number of fire and medical-related emergencies that were affected by the outage, and did it affect dispatch?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Additionally, the committee will focus on how and what type of training the department provides to both new and experienced personnel to handle such system disruptions.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Our goal is to ensure that the city's response to emergencies is expeditious and avoids any delays in answering and dispatching emergency calls.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: ground zero when the towers went down.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: My condolences for the loss of each and every one of your agencies, as well as those in the public who perished that day.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Feliz of the Public Safety Committee recognizes committee members and emphasizes that public safety is a core government responsibility. He notes New Yorkers rely on 911 during the most urgent and vulnerable moments of their lives and expect calls to be answered without delay.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz opens on public safety importance of reliable 911

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Oswald Feliz, Chair of the Committee on Public Safety.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I would like to thank all of today's co-chairs, Chair De La Rosa, Chair Areola, Chair Brewer, for co-chairing this oversight hearing, examining the seven-hour outage that occurred at one of our 911 call centers.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And I want to welcome everyone to today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I would also like to recognize members of the Public Safety Committee, Councilmember Justin Sanchez, Councilmember Wong, Areola, and Gutierrez.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Public safety is one of the most important responsibilities of city government.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Every minute of every day, New Yorkers rely on our 911 call system for emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They call for help from our police officers, firefighters, and emergency medical personnel during some of the most urgent and vulnerable moments of their lives.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: When someone calls,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: 911, they expect that call to be answered and that appropriate resources will be dispatched without delay.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What happened last month at the Bronx 911 call center, a seven-hour outage with very little to no notice to the public is unacceptable, and the city must explain what happened.

chapters.summary: Feliz describes the outage as starting at 3 a.m. and blocking calls for seven hours. He demands answers on what went wrong, why the update wasn't tested, why backup systems failed, and why the public was only notified seven hours later through the media rather than directly by the city.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz details August outage timeline and public notification failure

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: When people are facing an emergency, they should not have to wonder whether a 911 call will go through.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Reportedly, the outage was a result of updates that were made to service in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The updates went live at 3 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And they basically started blocking calls for seven hours between 3 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And 10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The city must explain what happened, including what went wrong, why wasn't the update tested before and after to ensure that it was working,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: what happened to the backup systems, which were supposed to reroute calls to the Brooklyn Center and instead allowed nearly 1,700 calls to go unanswered, and what steps will be taken to ensure that something like this never, ever happens again.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We also want to know, and this is equally important, why wasn't the public notified that the 911 system was not working?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Why did they only get notified seven hours later and they had to learn about this through the media rather than hearing about this directly from the city?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: People don't call 911 for fun.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They call when their safety is at risk, when they're in imminent danger, when they need immediate help from our police or fire department or medical services.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Technology can sometimes fail us.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We all know that.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Technology can sometimes fail us.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But failing to properly inform the public about something as important as the 911 system being out, that is not a technical glitch.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: That is a human choice, an unacceptable one.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: New Yorkers deserve to know when the 911 system is experiencing an outage so they can think about alternative ways of seeking help.

chapters.summary: Feliz notes the 911 system has had multiple outages: September 2024 due to a reconfiguration error, and 2022 when someone mistakenly pressed the power off button. He calls for ensuring the 911 system is safe from disruption and thanks agency staff and his committee team.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz recounts history of past 911 outages

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Now, our 911 call system has had outages, not only last month, last month a seven-hour outage, but also in September 2024, an outage due to a reconfiguration error.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And in 2022, when someone mistakenly pressed the power off button.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I look forward to discussing what steps we can take to ensure that our 911 system can always be a reliable system, one that is safe from disruption.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I want to thank the members of the NYPD, members of the Office of Technology and Innovation, the Fire Department, and all stakeholders for testifying today.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I also want to thank the staff, including the committee staff, for their hard work.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Josh Kingsley, Senior Counsel to the Committee, Chad Benjamin, Policy Analyst, Esperanza Diaz, my Chief of Staff, Santiago Baena, my Legislative Director, and also Dana and Sony from my team

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: who have joined, and I look forward to a productive conversation about today's topic.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, and I'll pass it back to Chair De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Felice.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We'll now hear from Chair Brewer.

utterances.text: I am Gail Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.text: I also want to thank Commissioner Golopta very, very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: New Yorkers rely, as we all know, on the 911 system.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In an emergency, we expect to be able to dial 911.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And receive immediate help.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Unfortunately for some who tried calling 911 on August 18th, as we know, that expectation was not met.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Filtering out alarms and duplicate calls, OTI estimates that around 400 callers may have been unable to reach emergency services, and I know you're still checking on that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The outage lasted for almost seven hours.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Once the outage was discovered, why were calls to the affected facility not rerouted to the Brooklyn facility?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: PSAC 1 and PSAC 2, supposed to work together.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And why did it take so long to bring them back up?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: These are questions that we need answered so that we can ensure that this never happens again.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And if it does,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: that we are better positioned to respond.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We cannot leave New Yorkers without access to emergency services for hours on end, as we know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: While the mayor has said that this is his first order of business, and I know it is, to resolve the call system, and that is his focus,

utterances.text: he can say that because I know he has a great staff and they are going to figure this out so it does not happen again.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Having been chair of the Technology Committee 100 years ago, when I was in the council previously, another era, I know that OTI, or then DOT, relied so many times on private companies for many tech issues.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In this case, I want to know how that partnership worked or did not work.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'd like to thank the following council staff for their work on this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: From the Government Operations Committee, Johari Frazier, Eric Cohen, and Sahid Hamid, and from my office, Cynthia Hornick, and everybody who has put this hearing together.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I'll turn it back to Chair De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want to also mention that Council Members Morano and Zhuang are here.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gelobter introduces herself and her colleagues. She describes the 911 system as the largest in the country, receiving over 9 million calls annually. The PSACs are governed cooperatively by OTI, NYPD, and FDNY with a shared mission of uninterrupted emergency operations. She notes the outage occurred on August 18, 2026.
chapters.title: CTO Gelobter: 911 system overview and PSAC governance structure

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair De La Rosa, Chair Felice, Chair Areola, Chair Brewer, and members of the City Council Committees on Technology, Public Safety, Fire and Emergency Management, and Government Operations, State and Federal Legislation.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I am Lisa Galopter, Chief Technology Officer for the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: And Commissioner of the Office of Technology and Innovation, also known as OTI.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Today I am joined by OTI Deputy Commissioner of Public Safety and Emergency Management, Robert Barbera,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: the FDNY Deputy Commissioner for Enterprise Technology and Chief Information Officer, Charles Jackson, and the NYPD's Chief of Staff, Ryan Marola,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Assistant Chief Richard Napolitano, and Executive Director Elizabeth Montemoros.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: As the largest and most complex emergency communication system in the country, New York City's 911 system receives over 9 million calls a year.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: The Public Safety Answering Centers, also known as PSAC, are governed cooperatively and collaboratively by OTI, the New York City Police Department, or NYPD,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: and the Fire Department of the City of New York, or FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: We have a singular shared mission to ensure expeditious, seamless, and uninterrupted emergency systems operations for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Any disruption to emergency communication services is of supreme concern.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: We join you today to discuss the disruption in New York City's 911 call service that occurred in the morning hours on Tuesday, August 18, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: First, I'll share some background context.

chapters.summary: Gelobter explains the 911 core services infrastructure is a managed service by Motorola Solutions, handling hardware and software that receives, routes, and delivers calls. She describes two physical locations—PSAC 1 in Brooklyn and PSAC 2 in the Bronx—each equipped to independently handle the full daily load of about 25,000 calls.
chapters.title: CTO Gelobter: Motorola managed service and call routing architecture

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: The 911 core services infrastructure is a managed service provided by vendor Motorola Solutions, Inc., MSI.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Core services means the hardware and software that receives a call from the originating service providers, the OSPs, also known as carriers.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: They account for the traffic patterns, it routes it to the proper location, and it delivers it to the call takers.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks for a NextGen 911 update, noting it has been in the works across three administrations. Gelobter says the current completion date is Q3 2027, having inherited a program the prior administration did not prioritize. chapters.title: De La Rosa questions NextGen 911 status and timeline delays

utterances.text: I want to pivot real quick before I pass the chair, Felice, to speak to, oh, and I want to recognize that Councilmember Maloney has done this.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: NextGen 911 is the city's effort to replace and modernize its aging 911 technology.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: The work began in 2020 and is now expected to be completed in 2027.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Now, I inherited this program that the last administration did not prioritize, but that's going to change under my watch.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: While in my experience, it's not unusual for a system this complex to encounter unexpected challenges in the stages of integration testing and user acceptance testing, and those naturally occur later in the process.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: This is a major multi-year overhaul that involves the NYPD, the FDNY, and other city agencies, and the transitioning is happening in phases so that 911 service can continue without interruption while the new system is put into place.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: However, as the new CTO, and I said this from the outset, which is my approach to leading OTI and making technology a strategic asset for the city, will include a disciplined review of every significant

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: We're going to be clear about why we're building it, what problem it solves, who it serves, and what measurable success looks like.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Then we will ensure that it delivers on time, cost-effectively, safely, and securely, without putting critical New Yorker-facing services, including 911, at risk.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So my expectation is straightforward.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what NextGen 911 will do differently. Gelobter explains E911 is legacy and analog, while NextGen 911 introduces digital systems that should streamline processes, improve logging, tracking, analysis, and alerting. Phase one rollout is the priority before additional modern features.

chapters.summary: Council Member Won asks how often firmware updates happen and whether the city tests them. Barbera confirms hundreds of updates happen per year, with test protocols before, during, and after changes. Won presses that testing failed to catch the issue. Barbera explains the issue surfaced an hour after the change completed, during a period when validation showed successful calls.

chapters.summary: Council Member Morano focuses on the human impact, noting that if someone is having a heart attack, they don't care about software. He asks how 911 calls began failing at 3:13 a.m. without the city knowing, what automated monitoring should have caught it, and why the first effective alarm was a call taker saying 'I can't hear somebody.'
chapters.title: Morano questions monitoring failure and hours-long detection gap

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to approach this a little differently because we could spend a lot of time today talking about software changes, routing environments, testing protocols, and...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Technical architecture.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But if you're the person having a heart attack, if someone's breaking into your house or your child isn't breathing, you don't care what piece of software malfunctioned, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You dial three numbers and you expect someone to answer.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And after hearing the testimony today, what concerns me most isn't simply that there was this technical failure.

utterances.text: It's how long the city appears to have gone without realizing the full extent of that failure.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So we've heard that the software change was completed, and based on what you told my colleague, Councilman Wong, we've heard

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: incredibly that the testing protocol was followed and that the problem manifested afterwards.

utterances.text: So my question is, if the system passed the city's testing protocol, how did 911 calls begin failing at 3.13 in the morning without the city knowing it was happening?

utterances.text: The issue wasn't escalated to Motorola and Verizon until about 7.30.

utterances.text: What automated monitoring should have caught that?

utterances.text: Was there an alarm, a dashboard?

utterances.text: And if those systems existed, why didn't they detect it?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: That is also not to say that we are not going to take a much closer look at what systems we can put in place.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: into place so that this would have been caught earlier going forward.

utterances.text: OTI working with the vendor began refining that list of numbers.

utterances.text: We didn't have to create any new jobs as a result of that contact.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks about researching what other cities do for backup routing and independent entities outside the police department. She also asks how the city plans to address distrust in the 911 system. Gelobter commits to looking at alternative routes, learning from other cities, and restoring trust through the root cause analysis and NextGen 911 implementation.

utterances.text: And that is what I'm committing to doing.

utterances.text: That means not just doing the root cause analysis, but also figuring out how we do implement NextGen 911 in a way that is timely as well as robust.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.text: You testified that those individuals were told to call.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What if they were deaf or hard of hearing?

utterances.text: I will let my colleague, DC Barbera, address that.

utterances.text: they would have other options for that community.

utterances.text: TTY was still available on voice services, as well as the deaf and hard of hearing community using translation apps that call in through national 911 into the city's 911 system.

utterances.speaker: Robert Barbera

chapters.summary: Abreu notes outages have happened at least twice this year and asks why there isn't a go-to policy for notifying the public. Gelobter says they are exploring policies and procedures including when and how New Yorkers get notified. Abreu presses on how fast an answer will come, fearing no procedure exists if an outage happens today. Gelobter says she's personally been in contact with NYSEM about Notify NYC.

utterances.text: Why is it that we don't have a go-to policy around when and whether to notify the public?

utterances.text: Twice this year alone means we shouldn't be debating what to do in the moment.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter

utterances.text: That is absolutely something that we have to explore as we're doing this root cause analysis.

utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I don't make it to seem like the root cause analysis is a future thing.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: We are in the process of working our way through all of the items.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I have personally been in contact with NYSOM around Notify NYC, figuring out what is the right process, what are the right policies, what would that message look like, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I don't have the final conclusions, but we are in the process of working with them to identify the best way forward.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa

chapters.summary: Council Member Stevens challenges Gelobter's references to the prior administration not prioritizing the system, asking what concrete steps this administration is taking differently. utterances.text: Good afternoon, I think.

utterances.text: And I know it was because you said that you were going to be looking more about transparency and all that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But like, even with this incident, there did not seem to be a lot of transparency and not informing the public, I believe, in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens

utterances.text: And what must change to address this going forward?

utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because it's...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If you don't give us a deadline, that means it can go on for a really long time, right?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so, like, what, in average, how long would an assessment take generally?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So an assessment for a system of this scale with this level of complexity with these number of stakeholders can take months.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: We are actively pursuing it, right, because, again, we are in a freeze state right now.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: And so every single change that has to go through has to go through an escalated level of scrutiny, which means that there is all these other things that are piling up that don't reach that level of

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: break change, necessary to be done immediately.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So we are trying to move as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: The only reason I'm hesitant to give you a specific deadline is because the way it works is you start analyzing, and then from that, there's 14 more questions that come up.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: And so I just, the more you dig, the more you learn, the more questions you have.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: And so I'm not trying to obfuscate the issue.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I just want to be able to give you a realistic answer.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Well, I think...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The realistic answer, and I'm sorry, I'm wrapping it right now.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I think the realistic answer is giving us a deadline, and then if you need to change it, then having those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm always uncomfortable when folks want to be so ambiguous, and then we have to leave to guess, right?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so there's no reason why you couldn't give us a deadline of when you think that this would be done because this is something that you're doing because we all know we have to be fluent.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so even if it's like, oh, we're looking at six months and then coming back to the council being like, then let's move forward because we're also accountable to the public as well, which is why I'm asking the questions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'm really not comfortable that it's like, well, we might come to hiccups.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You're going to come to hiccups.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And that's the point of these conversations.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so not trying to like bash you guys, but like we have to be on the same page of like when these operations are done so we can hold you accountable because that's literally our job.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Our job is to have oversight and ensure that you're doing your job.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I would just hope that you would have more concrete steps on how you're taking and moving things forward, what this is going to look like, and have deadlines so that we can come back and have real conversations.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: When it's so ambiguous, it makes me uncomfortable and seems like you're withholding information, not just from the council, but from the public, and that's unacceptable to me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Maloney, citing her technology sector experience, asks why Motorola deemed the upgrade low risk and why OTI didn't push back. Barbera explains the low-risk designation was based on calls being rerouted during the change. Maloney urges reevaluating risk criteria and questions why the full rollout proceeded and why internal metrics didn't catch the error.
chapters.title: Maloney questions low-risk designation and testing protocol failures

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Maloney, followed by Riley.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Commissioner, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Firmware upgrades in other municipalities or in New York City have caused issues in the past.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So why did Motorola...

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: ROLA deemed this a low risk when we're dealing with emergency services, and why didn't OTI push back on that designation?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I will answer at a top level and then I can let DC Barbera speak to additional levels of detail.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: As we mentioned earlier, there are hundreds of firmware upgrades in the course of a year.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Typically they are deemed low risk.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I think that

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: In this case, the thing that we have learned is we need to do a better job of understanding what the risk evaluation is.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: But I will hand off to DC Barbera.

utterances.speaker: Barbera
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Barbera
utterances.text: One of the key factors that's used in that risk evaluation is during the actual activity related to the change,

utterances.speaker: Barbera
utterances.text: Will calls for service be impacted?

utterances.speaker: Barbera
utterances.text: And because during this change, all call traffic was rerouted prior to the work happening, and there was no live traffic happening during that time period, it was deemed low risk because the traffic was routed to an alternate.

utterances.speaker: Barbera
utterances.text: location.

utterances.speaker: Barbera
utterances.text: At the completion of the change, the traffic was rerouted back and went under systematic testing over a period of time.

utterances.speaker: Barbera
utterances.text: But that's one of the factors that play into that low risk factor.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I urge you after this to reevaluate the criteria that we're using to determine risk.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks what role or liability Motorola has and what enforcement mechanisms exist. Gelobter says it's premature to ascribe specific responsibility before the root cause analysis. She confirms OTI manages the vendor, both OTI and Motorola track metrics, and the contract includes terms about contractor responsibilities and consequences for deficiencies.
chapters.title: Maloney questions Motorola's role, liability, and contract enforcement

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I worked in the technology sector before my role in city council, and before any major software rollout, we would test it in a test environment.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We would have pre-identified metrics that we were tracking to alert us right away whenever there was a delta from the norm, and this was 24-hour-a-day tracking, and we weren't doing emergency services.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So in this case, where the bar or the impact is so much higher, what can we do to better invest in a testing protocol?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: When those issues are identified, as it sounds like was in this case, why proceed with a full rollout?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And then why need to be notified by the NYPD or the customer, if you would, telling you when a system isn't working rather than internal metrics that could identify a system error or a bug that's occurred.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Council Member, for those questions.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I think the answer is there are testing protocols in place.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: It went through the validations.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: It was run through in the lab, and there was testing done during the rollout, and it did not catch the issue.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So that is where we need to go.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: go through and shore up the protocols, the analytics that we look at, the testing from soup to nuts, all the way through to the call recording testing.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: That sounds great.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And what role or liability does Motorola have in all this, if there's any information

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: you know, enforcement that we have to ensure that their software isn't producing these kinds of issues?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Until we have all the facts and we have completed the root cause analysis, it would be premature to ascribe specific responsibility and blame.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: What I can tell you that we do know today is that this system

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: was not prioritized with the former administration.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: It needs a full assessment.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Motorola did perform the firmware upgrade that triggered the issue.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: They were not aware that it broke.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: It took time for OTI to find and diagnose the problem and reroute the calls.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Because it's a complex system, it's really important that we look at all the contributing factors in minute detail.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: And I can guarantee you that we are going to use every shred of what we learn to make improvements and put more safeguards into place to prevent this type of issue from recurring.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: And in the meanwhile, we have also put precautions and extra precautions into place while the investigation is ongoing.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks who is responsible for tracking metrics and testing (both OTI and Motorola), who manages the vendor (OTI), and who communicates to the public during outages. Gelobter says NYSEM sends messages but the criteria and process for when they're notified need to be determined. Maloney asks who let NYSEM know and when—they became aware at 9:30 a.m. with 45 minutes of known impact.
chapters.title: Maloney questions responsibility for metrics, testing, and public communication

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Who is responsible for tracking those metrics and conducting testing?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Is it OTI or Motorola?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And who's responsible for managing the vendor?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: That would be OTI.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And we touched on this, but who's responsible for communicating to the public when there's an issue or an outage?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So I think that is one of the things in terms of the protocols and policies that we have to determine more comprehensively going forward.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Who makes those calls?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: NISM is the one who sends out the messages.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: And then how do they get notified?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: And based on what criteria is that decision made?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So just one last question is if NISM is responsible for communicating to the public currently, at least, who communicated with NISM and when were they made aware?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In order to communicate it more broadly.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: In this case, we became aware that there was an issue with New Yorkers calling 911 at about 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: It was remediated by about 10.19 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So it was about a 45-minute period where we knew that New Yorkers were being impacted.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: About 70% of the calls were still being answered.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So during that time frame, those 45 minutes, our main focus was on diagnosing the issue so that we could remediate it.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So the first 20 minutes or so,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: of that was trying to diagnose the source of the issue, and then the 25 minutes remaining were about rerouting calls to the systems that we knew were functioning.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And who is responsible for letting NYSEM know when there was an outage?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I think that is something that we need to be more specific about going forward, and that will be part of our analysis.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And looking forward to the root cause analysis.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Here's Council Member Riley.

chapters.summary: Council Member Riley, representing the Bronx, asks why calls didn't automatically transfer from PSAC 2 to PSAC 1 when the router failed. Gelobter confirms the cutover does not happen automatically for this type of situation, which is something they need to address going forward.
chapters.title: Riley questions why calls didn't automatically transfer from Bronx to Brooklyn

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and thank you, Commissioner, for testifying to the administration for coming out.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I don't want to beat a dead drum.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I know my colleagues have asked you questions and expressed their concerns.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I share a lot of concerns representing the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I know there were a lot of Bronx residents who were impacted by this outage.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So I just want to speak about the backup systems, if there are any.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: When the communication router failed, why didn't calls automatically transfer from PSEC 2 in the Bronx to the Brooklyn PSEC 1?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: While we do have monitoring in place and we have redundancies in place, the cut over does not happen automatically for a situation like this.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: And that is something that we need to figure out and understand what we can put into place going forward so that

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: a different outcome would happen next time.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What kind of backup system does the administration have in case this thing does happen again?

chapters.summary: Riley asks what backup systems exist if this happens again. Gelobter describes the fully redundant PSAC 1 and PSAC 2 architecture, additional redundancies she can't detail for security reasons, and interim measures including daily change management calls, deployment freeze, hourly manual call recording sampling, and PD call taker training on escalation.
chapters.title: Riley questions current backup systems and interim measures

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So today, so there's PSAC 1 and PSAC 2, which are fully redundant systems.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Each one has the capacity to manage individually every single emergency services call that might come in over the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So that's in place.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: There are additional redundancies within the architecture that are set up that I can't get into too much of the details for due to security concerns.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: But I will say additionally, we have put remediations into place at the moment, which includes things like daily change management calls to understand what needs to go out.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: We are in this freeze state.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: We are also doing monitoring of recordings on a manual basis, on an hourly basis.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So today, and we've also been training with the PD call takers to try to make sure that the escalation process for these, something similar like a dead air call, is escalated and

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: investigated and remediated as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I know Councilmember Manif spoke about the NYPD calls that happened during this time.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Are there any data on the FDNY and medical emergency calls that happened during this time as well?

chapters.summary: Riley asks if there's data on how many affected calls were fire or medical emergencies. FDNY responds they only know about calls transferred to them and are analyzing a list from OTI of callers who had issues and called back. They confirm there were no active fires that day.
chapters.title: Riley questions FDNY data on fire and medical calls during outage

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you just repeat that one time?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Out of the 1,700 effective calls that came in during the outage, is there any indication of how many of those were fire or medical emergencies?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So the way that it works, we're second seat in the dispatch process, so we would only know if the call actually came through to us.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We had asked OTI to provide us with a list of people that originally called, had the issue, and then called back and were able to get through, and we're in the process of analyzing those calls.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We just recently got it, so we're working on it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But we don't know specifically if there were any fires that took place.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: There were no fires.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: There were no active fires that day.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Notification, Commissioner, and I apologize and just, you know, you can educate me if this doesn't happen.

chapters.summary: Riley notes he learned about the outage from a news reporter, not from the administration. He asks if there's a protocol to alert council members so they can help navigate calls. Gelobter appreciates the question and says they will explore notifying appropriate stakeholders as part of their protocol review, and Riley urges them to utilize council members as partners.
chapters.title: Riley questions lack of notification to council members about outage

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I found out about this outage from a news reporter.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Typically when 911 calls aren't being answered, I don't know about everyone else's district, but I'm pretty sure people contact our offices after and we weren't really notified about this.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is there any protocol that the administration has moving forward that will alert members that these incidents are taking place so we could kind of figure out some ways that we can navigate some of these calls, if not all of these calls to the proper agencies that they belong to?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I really appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: And as we are thinking about the protocols for notifications, the criteria, and then also who should be notified,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I think that that is something that we should explore further, and we will definitely circle back with you on how we can make that most effective.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And utilize us as partners, because we definitely want to make sure that we're addressing this with you guys.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you so much for testifying, and thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Riley.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Councilmember Lincoln to close out first round, and then we'll go to Chair Felice for second round.

chapters.summary: Council Member Restler expresses deep concern about the outage's public safety implications. He asks if OTI, NYPD, and FDNY are working together on better testing. Gelobter confirms the root cause analysis will address testing, monitoring, change management, and communications, with a current freeze state on non-critical updates.
chapters.title: Restler questions testing protocols and preventing future outages

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair De La Rosa, and thank you for your tremendous leadership of our technology committee.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's good to see you all.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thanks for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I wanted to be here today because I was just so disturbed by the incident a few weeks ago and a shutdown of 911 operations, of 911 call intake operations in the Bronx at one of our two centers has just enormous implications for our public safety and stability.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And while it appears that this was an issue that relates to a Motorola upgrade and it was their fault and responsibility,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really do hope and expect that OTI, NPD, and FD are all working together to make sure that we have better testing in place, that this never happens again, that we prevent this type of...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Of outage that could have enormous public safety implications for us.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I do want to follow up on Councilmember Riley's questions from a moment ago around notifications.

chapters.summary: Restler notes that while real-time communication during an outage may be sensitive, the failure to reach out to stakeholders afterward was alarming and felt like an effort to shove it under the rug. He asks for a commitment to meaningful post-incident communication. Gelobter commits to identifying stakeholders, criteria, and mechanisms for notification.
chapters.title: Restler questions stakeholder communication after outage concluded

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, I can understand the sensitivity of publicizing the outage when it happens or while it is occurring and that there needs to be some deliberate

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: put into how, who you're communicating with in real time.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But at the conclusion of the outage, to not reach out to stakeholders and have conversations and explain what's going on was alarming.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it felt like there was an effort to kind of just shove it under the rug and not call attention to it because it was such an alarming and

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: troubling incident.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I'd love to just kind of push on his question once again.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do we have a commitment from this administration for more meaningful communication and coordination with stakeholders after, if, and I hope they do not, but if incidents occur relating to any 911 call center outages in the future?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: As we are doing this analysis, we will try to make a list of all of the stakeholders who should be notified and make sure, again, what the criteria is when a notification happens and by what mechanism

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: and making sure that the appropriate stakeholders are informed.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And in your review with Motorola, and I'm sure you've covered this at great length, so I'll do it briefly and then do one other question, but in your review with Motorola, are you confident that we won't see further issues with any upcoming upgrades?

chapters.summary: Restler asks if new protocols are in place for testing and redundancies during future upgrades. Gelobter says this is the crux of the root cause analysis—testing, monitoring, change management, and communications all need examination. She confirms the freeze state means only critical issues are being pushed.
chapters.title: Restler questions Motorola upgrade protocols and future testing

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And do we have new protocols in place for testing and redundancies to make sure that these incidents don't happen again when there are future upgrades happening to our technology?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: That is the crux of the issue.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: about what this root cause analysis is intended to address.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: We do have to explore the testing protocols, the monitoring protocols, the change management protocols, the communications, all of those things across the board.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Today, we are in a freeze state, meaning that only

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: the most critical issues are actually being pushed, which means that there are the things that are waiting in the wings until we can be really confident that as we're pushing stuff out, it will be successful.

chapters.summary: Restler asks why the Bronx location was affected. Gelobter explains Motorola pushed firmware to PSAC 2 firewalls deliberately, as PSAC 2 gets less traffic than PSAC 1, and rolling out one center at a time ensures the other remains unaffected. Call takers at both centers handled calls throughout.
chapters.title: Restler questions why Bronx PSAC 2 was impacted and not Brooklyn

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And why did this impact the Bronx location and not downtown Brooklyn?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: To be clear,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Each of the PSACs has different components.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: They both have a routing system, so hardware.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: They also have people, call takers.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So when Motorola did the original push of the firmware to the production systems, they were to the firewalls in the routing environment at PSAC 2.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: It was a conscious decision.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: PSAC 2 gets less traffic than PSAC 1.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So when you do a rollout, you want to roll out one center at a time to make sure that the other one is unaffected.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So that was a deliberate effort to make sure that both centers would not potentially be impacted if there was an issue.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Helpful.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Call takers at both centers were able to handle calls throughout the...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yes, understood.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Restler uses the opportunity to argue that PSAC 1's location in downtown Brooklyn's MetroTech campus is wrong, saying it closes off core streets and prevents the campus from being vibrant. He suggests the eastern Bronx location makes more sense and calls for reconsidering the downtown Brooklyn site. He acknowledges no one will respond today but says he's starting the push.
chapters.title: Restler advocates for relocating PSAC 1 from downtown Brooklyn

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Not entirely germane to the purpose of the hearing, but I have all of the relevant people at the DEA, so I'm going to use my soapbox opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think the PSAC 1 location is the wrong location.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And the idea of the Metro Tech campus is for it to be a dynamic, integrated part of the downtown Brooklyn community.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And the fact that we have PSAC there really closes off core streets of downtown Brooklyn and makes it impossible for people to get around.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We would welcome city agencies having a presence in those locations and those Metro Tech buildings, but I think it's the wrong spot for PSAC.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that the location that was built in the eastern Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: makes a ton of sense and is unlikely to have negative impacts on surrounding neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's an additive benefit.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In downtown Brooklyn, it really closes off an important part of a dynamic commercial hub.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And the Metro Tech campus is one of the only real campuses we have in the heart of kind of

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: the economic hubs of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it should be vibrant.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And instead, it is largely fenced, half of it, a third of it is fenced off because of the PSAC operations and FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really think that we should reconsider it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I imagine none of you are going to say anything about that today and that you've never even entertained the idea, but I'm making a push.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's coming.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's starting right now.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Oh, and we've been joined by my neighbor to the north, Councilmember Dinnowitz.

chapters.summary: Council Member Dinowitz asks about the May texting outage. Barbera explains it was caused by a larger system upgrade after six years live, and took 110 minutes to resolve because many components had to be reverted. Dinowitz asks how many minor outages occur; Gelobter says only the May and August incidents impacted New Yorkers in 2026.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions cause and duration of May text-to-911 outage

utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: My neighbor, too.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks about the NYPD's 6 a.m. notification. Elizabeth describes how a call taker experienced multiple calls with no audio from the same caller ID, and a neighboring call taker was told by a caller they couldn't get through to 911 and 311 transferred them. utterances.text: Going back to that 6 a.m.

utterances.text: Notification and the 6.40 a.m.

utterances.text: Ticket.

utterances.text: So you were the first to notify about potential issues, correct?

utterances.text: What were some of the issues that you experienced during that time?

utterances.text: One of our call takers experienced multiple calls in a short period of time in the same caller ID where they were unable to hear the caller on the other side.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: If somebody's in a bad area for cell service, you can get through and you don't hear them.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So it's not like this never happens.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It only raised their alarm because it happened several times in a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So those two call takers did exactly what they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: They brought it to the principal, who then ran it up the chain and notified OTI and got the whole investigation going.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But that's how it all started.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I hope I answered your question.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks for a ballpark of affected calls. Elizabeth reports 322 calls with one-way audio from the 10-digit alarm number between 3:13 a.m. and 6 a.m., presented to 83 unique call takers. utterances.speaker: Elizabeth
utterances.text: I have the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks what steps were taken. Gelobter explains teams looked at hardware, headsets, and position-specific issues. Barbera adds they triaged what was believed to be a looping alarm auto-dialer, engaged Verizon for alarm routing, and escalated when the broader scope became clear.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We knew that it wasn't just alarm companies having some issues with the...

utterances.text: At that time, the reported issue was with that same caller ID, which is the 10-digit emergency alarm number.

utterances.text: Can you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't catch the response.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth
utterances.text: The second response or the full response?

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: The second response.

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth
utterances.text: At that time, the reported issue was with that same caller ID, the 10-digit alarm emergency number.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, and can you repeat again what steps were taken to resolve the issue?

utterances.speaker: Elizabeth
utterances.text: I deferred.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: OTI.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So between, starting at 6 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: When there was the shoulder tap identifying the issues that the call takers were presenting at those two positions,

utterances.text: there were a number of elements looked at, including looking at hardware, headsets, and all of those types of things.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: I don't know, DC Barbera, if you want to provide any more color.

utterances.speaker: Barbera
utterances.text: So from the time that the initial issue was reported at those two positions, technical teams began troubleshooting those positions.

utterances.speaker: Barbera
utterances.text: Obviously, there could be a number of technical problems that could be impacting audio conditions.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks how often updates occur and whether this was major or minor. Barbera says it was minor, with updates almost daily—2,800 changes in 2025 without impact. Dinowitz asks how management can be improved. Gelobter says they're examining governance, risk assessment, technical processes, policies, and communications.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions update frequency and 911 management improvements

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How often do you update your systems?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Would you say weekly, monthly, every year?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And also, what type of update was this?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Would you say this was a major update or just a minor one?

utterances.speaker: Barbera

utterances.speaker: Barbera
utterances.text: And to give you an example of that, in calendar year 2025, we executed 2,800 changes within the environment without impact.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What are ways that you think the management of the 911 system can be improved?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think earlier you implied that there's a lot of room for improvement.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What are some of the conversations that you've had on that?

utterances.text: Is it having less people involved, less agencies and offices?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Yes, we are, as part of this deep dive, we are looking at not just technical processes as well as policies, procedures, process communications.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: We are looking at the governance structure.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: We are how should risk assessment be evaluated.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So I think that there are a number of factors that we're going to look at across the board.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks what systems exist to know if systems are online or if there's an outage. Gelobter confirms monitoring exists at different infrastructure levels but can't detail for security reasons. She adds interim manual measures including hourly call recording sampling and PD call taker training on dead air call escalation.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions monitoring systems for detecting outages

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What are systems that we have in place currently to let us know whether the systems we have are online or there's an outage?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: There is current monitoring systems at different levels of the infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: And again, I can't get into too much detail on that because of security concerns.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: But in addition to the technological monitoring that is in place, we have all of the agencies are working together collaboratively to ensure that there are

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: manual systems today that will be looking at looking to try to capture any of these issues that might reoccur.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Gelobter
utterances.text: So whether that is manually or hourly sampling call recordings, we are working with the PD call takers to figure out what the right criteria is

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: to escalate what I would term dead air calls, and then as well what that process should be to investigate them and deliver a substantiation of the issue.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So there are a number of things that we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: There are already some things that we have put into place in the interim, and then we also need to figure out the long-term strategy.

chapters.summary: Morano asks who independently verifies Motorola's account, noting Motorola performed the change, diagnosed the problem, helped restore service, and is now analyzing the root cause of its own failure. He asks if any outside technical expert, comptroller, or inspector general is reviewing the evidence. Gelobter says she is personally overseeing it and they need to ensure Motorola delivers to required standards.
chapters.title: Morano questions independent verification of Motorola's root cause analysis

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: All right, no more questions.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But yeah, I just want to say, yeah, we have a lot of work to do on this issue, including and especially on basic things, including notifying the public.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Again, people, when they have an emergency, when they're facing a fire or could potentially become the victim of an assault or any other crime, we tell them to call 911.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Every second counts, as we all know, and them not knowing, not being notified, or us not even making a good faith effort to notify people about an outage in the 911 system, that is just alarming, it's disturbing, and

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: not a good example of good government.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And also, so look forward to working on the notification part.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And also, just got to say, I know we've done a lot, and I know this is on all of us as a city, but the fact that we wouldn't even be able to tell whether calls are getting transferred to the Brooklyn Center or the Bronx Center is out.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And also, it seems like we don't even know whether there's an outage or not.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: It seems like we're just dealing with a really hot mess, which we have to give a lot of attention to.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Councilmember Morano, followed by Wong.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner, thank you for being so diligent with your answers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I know this has gone on a while, but obviously it's an important issue.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to focus on something a little different.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We've talked about what Motorola did.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What I'd like to understand is who independently verifies Motorola's account of what happened?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Motorola is a major contractor on this system.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Motorola performed the software change.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They participated in diagnosing the problem.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They helped restore the service.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is Motorola also participating in determining the root cause of the failure associated with its own change?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And if so, who is independently validating that conclusion for the city?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is there some sort of outside technical expert, the controller or an inspector general, cyber command, really anybody without a financial relationship with Motorola reviewing the underlying evidence?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Motorola is performing their own internal analysis as we speak.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: in terms of validating and vetting that,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The answer I want to give is me.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: At this point, right, trying to figure out what happened and how we prevent it from happening again, especially given that they are such a major vendor and provider of service for us,

utterances.text: is something that we need to take a closer look at and really understand.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: If they are going to be a managed service provider, they need to make sure that they are delivering to the standards that are required.

utterances.text: Right, particularly when the city's gone from paying them 20-some-odd million dollars to around $80 million.
